title: Surfaces described by two parameters
objectives: Parametrise a surface and compute its area element.

screens.title: A sheet on a cylinder
screens.prose: A flat rubber sheet carries a grid: $\theta$ across from 0 to $2\pi$, $z$ up from 0 to 3. We wrap it round a cylinder of radius 2, so the point $(\theta, z)$ lands at $(2\cos\theta,\ 2\sin\theta,\ z)$. Rotate the cylinder to see all four patches.
screens.question: Tap the patch where the marked cell lands.

hints.text: The cell runs from $\theta = 1.5$ to $2.1$ and from $z = 2$ to $2.5$.
Height is $z$ itself: the patch sits between 2 and 2.5 up.
Angle 1.5 to 2.1 starts at about a quarter turn from the $x$-axis, counterclockwise from above.

feedback.correct: The cell keeps its height and turns through its angle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the patch at height 2 to 2.5 and angle 1.5 to 2.1.

byKey.swap: That patch swaps the roles of $\theta$ and $z$. The angle goes round, the height goes up.
byKey.mirror: That patch measures the angle clockwise. $\theta$ runs counterclockwise seen from above.
byKey.flip: That patch measures height down from the top. $z$ is the height above the floor.

explain.text: The map keeps $z$ and wraps $\theta$ round the circle of radius 2. So the cell lands at height 2 to 2.5, from about a quarter turn on.

screens.title: How much it stretches
screens.prose: The marked cell is $0.6$ wide in $\theta$ and $0.5$ tall in $z$. On the cylinder its height is still $0.5$. Its width becomes an arc of the circle of radius 2.
screens.question: By what factor is the cell's area stretched?

options.why: You kept the width, but an angle step $d\theta$ becomes an arc $2\,d\theta$ long.
You squared the radius as for a disc. Only the width stretches; the height stays.
You used the whole circumference. One unit of $\theta$ is an arc of length 2, not $2\pi$.

hints.text: An arc of angle $d\theta$ on a circle of radius 2 has length $2\,d\theta$.
Width times 2, height times 1: area times 2.

feedback.correct: The width doubles and the height stays, so the area doubles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the cell's width and height before and after.

byKey.one: This map is a pure bending only at radius 1. Here the arc is $2 \times 0.6 = 1.2$.
byKey.four: Only one direction stretches. The height $0.5$ is unchanged.
byKey.twopi: One unit of angle is a radius-length of arc: 2, not $2\pi$.

explain.text: The cell's width $0.6$ becomes an arc $1.2$ long, and its height stays $0.5$. Its area goes from $0.3$ to $0.6$, a factor of 2.

screens.title: Two tangent vectors
screens.prose: A **parametric surface** is a map $\mathbf r(u, v)$ from a flat domain into space. Its **tangent vectors** are $\mathbf r_u$ and $\mathbf r_v$, the partial derivatives. Here $\mathbf r(\theta, z) = (2\cos\theta,\ 2\sin\theta,\ z)$. Move $\theta$ and watch $\mathbf r_\theta$ stay tangent to the circle.
screens.question: What is $\mathbf r_\theta$ at $\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$? Give $(a, b, c)$.

hints.text: Differentiate each entry of $\mathbf r$ with respect to $\theta$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate each entry in $\theta$, then put $\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.

byKey.point: That is the point $\mathbf r$ itself, not its derivative.

explain.text: $\mathbf r_\theta = (-2\sin\theta,\ 2\cos\theta,\ 0)$ has length 2 at every $\theta$, the stretch we found. $\mathbf r_z = (0, 0, 1)$ has length 1. A cell $d\theta\,dz$ maps to a parallelogram with sides $\mathbf r_\theta\,d\theta$ and $\mathbf r_z\,dz$.

screens.title: The cross product
screens.prose:
We need the area of a slanted parallelogram. The **cross product** does it: $$\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1 - a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2 - a_2b_1).$$
It is at right angles to $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, and its length is the parallelogram's area.
screens.question: What is $(1, 0, 2) \times (0, 1, 3)$? Give $(a, b, c)$.

hints.text: Third: $a_1b_2 - a_2b_1 = 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0$. Check both dot products are 0.

feedback.correct: $(-2, -3, 1)$. Its dot products with $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are $-2 + 2 = 0$ and $-3 + 3 = 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the three entries one at a time.

byKey.swap: You computed $\mathbf b \times \mathbf a$. Swapping the order flips the sign.
byKey.mult: You multiplied entry by entry. The cross product mixes the entries in pairs.

explain.text: The entries are $0 - 2$, $0 - 3$ and $1 - 0$. Both dot products are 0, so $(-2, -3, 1)$ is at right angles to the parallelogram. Its length $\sqrt{14} \approx 3.742$ is the parallelogram's area.

screens.title: Which way it points
screens.prose: Two directions are at right angles to the parallelogram. The **right-hand rule** picks one. Curl the fingers of your right hand from $\mathbf a$ towards $\mathbf b$; the thumb gives $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$. Rotate the view to check.
screens.question: Which way does $\mathbf b \times \mathbf a$ point?

options.text: Along $(2, 3, -1)$, the other side of the parallelogram
Along $(-2, -3, 1)$, the same as $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$
options.why: You kept the order of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. Curling from $\mathbf b$ to $\mathbf a$ turns the thumb over.
That lies in the parallelogram. A cross product is at right angles to both vectors.

hints.text: Curl from $\mathbf b$ towards $\mathbf a$ this time.
Reversing the curl reverses the thumb.

feedback.correct: Swapping the order turns the thumb round: $\mathbf b \times \mathbf a = (2, 3, -1)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Curl your fingers from $\mathbf b$ towards $\mathbf a$.

byKey.same: Order matters: $\mathbf b \times \mathbf a = -(\mathbf a \times \mathbf b)$.
byKey.inplane: $\mathbf a + \mathbf b$ is a diagonal of the parallelogram, not a normal.

explain.text: Each entry of the formula changes sign when $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ swap. So $\mathbf b \times \mathbf a = (2, 3, -1)$, the same length pointing the other way.

screens.title: The area element
screens.prose: Let $\mathbf r(u, v)$ be smooth and one-to-one on a domain $D$, apart from a set of no area. We find the surface's area.
screens.question: Put the derivation in order. Leave out the flawed line.

lines.text: A cell $du$ by $dv$ maps, to first order, to a parallelogram with sides $\mathbf r_u\,du$ and $\mathbf r_v\,dv$. (Linear approximation of $\mathbf r$.)
A parallelogram with sides $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ has area $|\mathbf a \times \mathbf b|$. (Length of the cross product.)
So the patch has area $|\mathbf r_u \times \mathbf r_v|\,du\,dv$. (Scalars come out of a cross product.)
Adding patches and letting the cells shrink: $\text{area} = \iint_D |\mathbf r_u \times \mathbf r_v|\,du\,dv$. (A Riemann sum becomes the integral.)
The patch has area $|\mathbf r_u|\,|\mathbf r_v|\,du\,dv$. (Length times width.)
lines.why: That is right only when $\mathbf r_u$ and $\mathbf r_v$ are at right angles. A slanted parallelogram has less area.

hints.text: The cell's image is a parallelogram.
Its area is the length of a cross product.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Go from one cell, to its parallelogram, to its area, to the sum.

byKey.d1: Length times width is the area of a rectangle only. The cross product allows for the slant.
byKey.left-out: All four true lines are needed.

explain.text: Each cell becomes a parallelogram with sides $\mathbf r_u\,du$ and $\mathbf r_v\,dv$. Its area is $|\mathbf r_u \times \mathbf r_v|\,du\,dv$, written $dS$. For the cylinder $|\mathbf r_\theta \times \mathbf r_z| = 2$.

screens.title: The whole cylinder
screens.prose: For the cylinder, $\mathbf r_\theta \times \mathbf r_z = (2\cos\theta,\ 2\sin\theta,\ 0)$, of length 2, pointing straight out. The domain is $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, $0 \le z \le 3$.
screens.question: What is the area of the curved side?

hints.text: Integrate $|\mathbf r_\theta \times \mathbf r_z| = 2$ over the domain.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the stretch 2 by the domain's area $6\pi$.

byKey.no-stretch: $6\pi$ is the flat sheet's area. Each cell doubles when it wraps.
byKey.lids: You added the two discs at the ends. The question asks for the curved side only.

explain.text: The integrand is the constant 2 over a domain of area $6\pi$. So the side has area $12\pi \approx 37.70$, which is circumference $4\pi$ times height 3.

screens.title: A graph
screens.prose:
A graph $z = f(x, y)$ is the surface $\mathbf r = (x, y, f(x, y))$. Then $\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y = (-f_x,\ -f_y,\ 1)$, so $$dS = \sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2}\,dA.$$
Take the plane $z = 2x + 3y$ over the unit square.
screens.question: What is its area, to 3 decimal places?

hints.text: The square has area 1, so the area is $\sqrt{14}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $f_x$ and $f_y$, then take $\sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2}$.

byKey.no-root: You left out the square root. The length is $\sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2}$.
byKey.shadow: That is the shadow's area. The tilted plane has more.
byKey.no-one: You left out the 1 from the $z$ entry of $(-f_x, -f_y, 1)$.

explain.text: $\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y = (-2, -3, 1)$, the cross product we computed. Its length $\sqrt{14}$ is constant, so the area is $\sqrt{14} \approx 3.742$ times the square's area 1.

screens.title: The sphere
screens.prose: The unit sphere is $\mathbf r(\phi, \theta) = (\sin\phi\cos\theta,\ \sin\phi\sin\theta,\ \cos\phi)$, $0 \le \phi \le \pi$, $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$. Then $|\mathbf r_\phi \times \mathbf r_\theta| = \sin\phi$. That is $\rho^2\sin\phi$ at $\rho = 1$, from spherical coordinates.
screens.question: What is the sphere's area?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $\sin\phi$ over $\phi$, then over $\theta$.

byKey.half: $2\pi$ is one hemisphere. $\phi$ runs from 0 to $\pi$, pole to pole.

explain.text: The $\phi$ integral gives $[-\cos\phi]_0^\pi = 2$, and the $\theta$ integral gives $2\pi$. So the area is $4\pi$.

screens.title: The missing stretch
screens.prose: A classmate finds the sphere's area as $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi d\phi\,d\theta$, the area of the flat domain.
screens.question: What do they get, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the classmate's integral as written.

byKey.right: That is the true area. The classmate's integral has no $\sin\phi$ in it.
byKey.dot: That is what $\mathbf r_\phi \cdot \mathbf r_\theta$ gives: the two vectors are at right angles. The area element is a cross product.

explain.text: Without $|\mathbf r_\phi \times \mathbf r_\theta| = \sin\phi$ the integral measures the flat domain, $2\pi^2 \approx 19.74$. Near the poles the domain's cells shrink to slivers on the sphere, so the domain overcounts. The true area is $4\pi$.

screens.title: Poles and double cover
screens.prose: At the poles $\mathbf r_\phi \times \mathbf r_\theta = \mathbf 0$: a whole edge of the domain pinches to one point. The area $4\pi$ is still right, since a point has no area. Now a classmate lets $\theta$ run from 0 to $4\pi$ and gets $8\pi$.
screens.question: What went wrong?

options.text: The map covers the sphere twice; it must be one-to-one apart from a set of no area
The poles, where the cross product is $\mathbf 0$, add extra area
options.why: You blamed the pinch. Two points have no area, and $\sin\phi = 0$ adds nothing there.

options.text: Nothing: area depends on the parametrisation
options.why: Area belongs to the surface. Any smooth parametrisation, one-to-one apart from a set of zero area, gives $4\pi$.

hints.text: Follow a point as $\theta$ goes from $2\pi$ to $4\pi$.

feedback.correct: Each point is reached twice, so each patch is counted twice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many times each point of the sphere is reached.

byKey.poles: The pinch is real but harmless: the integrand $\sin\phi$ is 0 there.
byKey.param: Two parametrisations, each one-to-one apart from a set of zero area, give the same area.

explain.text: From $2\pi$ to $4\pi$, $\theta$ retraces every circle of latitude. The integral counts the sphere twice: $8\pi$. The poles are harmless, since a point or a seam has no area.

screens.title: Random portfolios
screens.prose: Fully invested long-only weights in three assets satisfy $w_1 + w_2 + w_3 = 1$, $w_i \ge 0$: a triangle in space. Backtests compare a strategy with random portfolios drawn uniformly on it. Write it as the graph $w_3 = 1 - w_1 - w_2$ over its shadow.
screens.question: What is the triangle's area, to 3 decimal places?

hints.text: The shadow is a right triangle of area $\tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $\sqrt3$ by the shadow's area.

byKey.shadow: That is the shadow's area. The tilted triangle is $\sqrt3$ times larger.
byKey.no-half: You used a unit square as the shadow. The shadow is half of it.

explain.text: With $f = 1 - w_1 - w_2$, $dS = \sqrt3\,dA$. The shadow has area $\tfrac12$, so the triangle has area $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \approx 0.866$. It is equilateral with side $\sqrt2$, which agrees.

ideas: A parametric surface $\mathbf r(u, v)$ has tangent vectors $\mathbf r_u$, $\mathbf r_v$; a cell $du\,dv$ maps to a parallelogram with those sides.
$\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$ is at right angles to both, with length the parallelogram's area; order sets its direction by the right-hand rule.
For $\mathbf r$ smooth and one-to-one apart from a set of no area, $\text{area} = \iint_D |\mathbf r_u \times \mathbf r_v|\,du\,dv$; a graph gives $\sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2}$.
summary.trap: Integrating $du\,dv$ without $|\mathbf r_u \times \mathbf r_v|$ measures the flat domain: $2\pi^2$ for the sphere, not $4\pi$.

quiz.prose: The paraboloid $z = x^2 + y^2$ for $z \le 1$ has $dS = \sqrt{1 + 4r^2}\,r\,dr\,d\theta$ in polar form.
quiz.question: What is its area, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute $s = 1 + 4r^2$ in the $r$ integral.

byKey.disc: That is the area of the shadow, the unit disc.

quiz.prose: The cone $z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ has $f_x^2 + f_y^2 = 1$ away from its tip.
quiz.question: What is the area of the part with $z \le 1$, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $dS = \sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2}\,dA$.

byKey.disc: That is the shadow's area. The cone is tilted at 45 degrees.
byKey.no-root: You used $1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2 = 2$ without the square root.

explain.text: $\sqrt{1 + 1} = \sqrt2$ is constant, and the shadow is the unit disc. The area is $\sqrt2\,\pi \approx 4.443$; the tip is one point and adds nothing.

quiz.question: Which $\mathbf r(u, v)$ is the cone $z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$, $z \le 1$?

options.text: $(u\cos v,\ u\sin v,\ u)$, $0 \le u \le 1$, $0 \le v \le 2\pi$

options.why: That keeps the radius at 1: a cylinder. On the cone the radius grows with height.
That is the unit sphere. Its points are all at distance 1 from the origin.
That has $z = r^2$: the paraboloid, not the cone.

feedback.correct: At radius $u$ the height is $u$, which is $z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check that $z$ equals the distance from the $z$-axis.

byKey.cyl: The radius must grow with height.

explain.text: $x^2 + y^2 = u^2$ and $z = u \ge 0$, so $z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$. The ranges give the part with $z \le 1$.

quiz.prose: A flat map $\mathbf r(u, v) = (x(u, v),\ y(u, v),\ 0)$ has $\mathbf r_u \times \mathbf r_v = (0,\ 0,\ x_uy_v - x_vy_u)$.
quiz.question: What is $|\mathbf r_u \times \mathbf r_v|$ for such a map?

options.text: $|J|$, the Jacobian from changes of variables

options.why: A flat map can still stretch: polar coordinates stretch by $r$.
You took lengths of separate partials. The cross product's third entry is a determinant.

feedback.correct: The area element of a surface generalises the Jacobian.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the third entry of the cross product.

byKey.one: Polar coordinates are a flat map with stretch $r$.
byKey.sum: The entry is $x_uy_v - x_vy_u$, a determinant.

explain.text: The only entry is $x_uy_v - x_vy_u$, the Jacobian determinant. So $dS = |J|\,du\,dv$, as in a change of variables; polar coordinates give $r$.

quiz.prose: A uniform random portfolio has density 2 on the shadow triangle in the $(w_1, w_2)$ plane, of area $\tfrac12$.
quiz.question: What density per unit of surface area on the tilted triangle integrates to 1?

options.why: You kept the flat density. The tilted triangle has $\sqrt3$ times the area.
You multiplied by the stretch. More area means a thinner density.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the flat density by the stretch $\sqrt3$.

explain.text: Probability is the same on a patch and its shadow, and $dS = \sqrt3\,dA$. So the density per unit of surface area is $\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$, and $\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3} \times \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = 1$.
